claims.text: The as-cast alloy is a non-equilibrium, supersaturated solid solution containing metastable mixed phases.
Annealing at 400–600°C can initiate partial diffusion-driven phase separation without reaching full equilibrium.
Thermal energy promotes diffusion of Mg and other alloy constituents.
Mg segregation produces localized Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
The Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates form coherent interfaces with the surrounding solid solution.
The intermetallic precipitates act as nucleation sites or barriers for oxide formation.
The precipitate-modified microstructure stabilizes a protective high-temperature oxide scale.
The annealed alloy develops a more stable and adherent oxide scale than the as-cast alloy.
Annealing improves high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast baseline.
The precipitates alter local passivity at phase boundaries.
The modified phase distribution creates or disrupts galvanic coupling at phase boundaries.
Changes in local electrochemical conditions alter corrosion behavior.
Annealing produces a measurable corrosion-rate difference relative to the as-cast state, although the direction is unspecified.
The proposed effect is limited to a 400–600°C processing window that induces partial phase separation.
Full equilibration outside the proposed processing window may erase the beneficial microstructural features.
An inert annealing atmosphere prevents premature oxidation.
The studied alloy is constrained to a density below 6 g/cm³.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as containing metastable mixed phases, while the baseline is described as a homogeneous supersaturated solid solution. A homogeneous single solution and an already mixed-phase microstructure are not equivalent, so the reference state is internally ambiguous.
